requested.title: Unknown chain `op` throws TypeError instead of returning invalid-payload
Duplicate-entry rejection in computeVariablesDigest uses JS string identity, not the encoded UTF-8 bytes it actually hashes
contextInvalidField does not reject an empty variableId, unlike every sibling coordinate field

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: Verified in the current source. `checkFraming` (chain-verify.ts:102-120) validates suite, seq, the genesis/seq-1 coupling and prev_hash, but never validates that `entry.op` is one of the eight known operations. `checkPayloadShape` (L126-146) validates timestamp, actor, signature and that payload is a record, then calls `operationShapeOk` (L247-249), which does an unguarded `PAYLOAD_SHAPES[entry.op](entry.payload as never)`. For an unknown op string (or a non-string op) at seq > 1 the lookup yields `undefined` and the invocation raises a TypeError. There is no try/catch anywhere in `verifyChainCore`'s loop (L682-699) — the only try/catch in the file is inside `verifyEntrySignature`, which is reached *after* the shape check — so the throw escapes `verifyChain`. That directly contradicts the exported JSDoc at L722-724 ('Entries are treated as untrusted input … so malformed data yields `invalid-payload` instead of throwing') and the file-level comment at L60-63 which states the whole design rule for this module. I also confirmed a second, worse variant the report only implies: because `PAYLOAD_SHAPES` is a plain object literal, `op` values that hit `Object.prototype` (`"toString"`, `"constructor"`, `"valueOf"`) resolve to a *callable* inherited method that returns a truthy value, so the shape gate passes; `applyOperation` (L551-574) then falls off its non-default switch returning `undefined`, and `if (applied !== null)` treats `undefined` as a failure, producing `fail(undefined)` — a ChainInvalid error with an `undefined` reason code. Both branches are contract violations. On exploitability I agree with the reporter and confirmed it independently: `ChainEntrySchema` (packages/api-schema/src/chain.ts) is a union of eight `Schema.Literal`-discriminated structs, and every production entry path goes through it — the append endpoint decodes wire entries with it before `chain-accept.ts` calls `verifyChainEffect`, and stored entries in `chain-store.ts:62` are `JSON.parse`d from rows that were only ever written post-decode. So there is no attacker-reachable path today. It remains a genuine defect: `chain-store.ts:135-147` lifts the verifier via `Effect.promise` and dies on anything that isn't a ChainInvalid, so a throw here would surface as a DO defect/500 rather than the specified 422 — exactly the outcome the no-throw contract exists to prevent. BUG severity is correct; this is a defence-in-depth/contract gap, not a vulnerability.

The mechanical claim is accurate: `computeVariablesDigest` (manifest-sign.ts:93-103) keys its duplicate `Set` on the raw JS string, while the digest bytes come from `encodeLengthPrefixed([entry.variableId, …])` (L108-113) → `utf8Encode` → `TextEncoder.encode` (bytes.ts:6-8), and per the WHATWG encoding spec TextEncoder maps every unpaired surrogate to U+FFFD (EF BF BD). So `"\uD800"`, `"\uDFFF"` and `"\uFFFD"` would be three distinct Set keys that hash to identical bytes, and `compareVariableIdBytes` (L65-76) would likewise report 0 for them. But the precondition — a variable id containing a lone surrogate — cannot be reached. I traced every id source: `VariableIdSchema` in packages/core/src/project.ts:46-50 pins ids to `/^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$/`, pure ASCII with no surrogate representable, and it is applied at every API boundary (data.ts:62/127, data-api.ts:69/99/111, rotation-api.ts:48/59). The server's digest inputs come from `data-store.ts` `variableDigestEntries`, reading `variable_id` columns that were only ever written through those schema-validated endpoints. The CLI's inputs (`apps/cli/src/manifest.ts:102`) come from HttpApi-derived, schema-decoded responses carrying the same `VariableIdSchema`. Over the entire reachable id alphabet, UTF-8 encoding is injective, so the Set-key/digest-byte mismatch is a distinction without a difference: dedup, sort order and digest all agree. No attacker-controllable path produces two entry sets with a colliding `variables_digest_hex`, so no manifest signature can be transplanted. The function's own contract also frames duplicates as 'a caller bug' rather than an untrusted-input boundary (unlike chain-verify.ts, which explicitly promises safety against hostile server-distributed data), so this is not even a self-contract violation. The suggested hardening (`isWellFormed()`, or keying the Set on `encodeHex(utf8Encode(id))`) is reasonable belt-and-braces, but as a finding this is not exploitable and not a defect under any reachable input.

Confirmed by direct comparison of the two files. `contextInvalidField` in value-sign.ts:100-117 checks `suite`, `projectId`, `environmentId` and `writerUserId` for non-emptiness, then delegates to `numericFieldInvalid` and `hexFieldInvalid` — `context.variableId` is never checked, despite being a signed coordinate emitted at buildValueSignedBytes L136. The sibling module meta-sign.ts:123-124 applies exactly the analogous check (`context.target.kind === "variable" && context.target.variableId.length === 0` → `"context variableId"`), so the omission is an inconsistency inside the same crypto layer, not a deliberate asymmetry. The in-file comment at L104-106 makes the intent explicit: the non-empty checks on projectId/environmentId exist 'for defensive consistency … to hold the other fields to the same check level', which is precisely the rule variableId escapes. `valueContextInvalidField` is the shared gate for `computeValueSignedBytesHash`, `signValue` and `verifyValueSignature`, so all three accept an empty variableId. I agree with the reporter that this is not a forgery path: `encodeLengthPrefixed` (encoding.ts) writes a uint32-BE length before every field, so an empty variableId encodes unambiguously as a zero-length field and cannot be confused with a shifted neighbouring coordinate — there is no canonicalization ambiguity to exploit. Nor is it externally reachable, since `VariableIdSchema` forbids the empty string at the API boundary. What remains is a real missing defensive check: a caller bug that would produce a value statement signed at a coordinate with no variable is silently signed instead of being rejected as InvalidInput, which is exactly the class of caller bug the sibling checks were added to catch. The one-line fix the reporter proposes is correct. BUG severity is appropriate.
